provenance.other: “exceeding good land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 14:7 — Joshua and Caleb's minority report. 'Spy out' occurs in ten KJV verses, of which six belong to Numbers 13 and Judges 18, so the verb alone identifies no source; what identifies one is the sequence in which it stands here.
provenance.significance: Numbers 13-14 is the Bible's one story of a spy who comes back with a good report and is nearly killed for it. Twelve men are sent to spy out the land; ten bring an evil report; two say it is an exceeding good land; and the congregation bids stone them (14:10). Mosiah 9:1-2 is that story with one man: Zeniff is sent to spy out the Lamanites' forces, sees 'that which was good among them', contends with his brethren for a treaty, and is condemned to death and rescued. The metalepsis cuts against Zeniff. In Numbers the favourable report is the true one and the men who give it are the only two of their generation to enter the land; here the favourable report begins a chapter that ends in slaughter and a book that ends in bondage — and Limhi has already told the reader at 7:21 that Zeniff was deceived.

9:1.note: 'I having been sent as a spy among the Lamanites, that I might spy out their forces … but when I saw that which was good among them, I was desirous that they should not be destroyed.' The verbal contact is thin and deliberate — 'spy out' and 'good' — and the case is made by the scene, which the KJV tells once. Zeniff's own account is at pains to make him Caleb: the lone dissenter who saw good where his brethren saw a target. What follows in the next verse is the stoning that Numbers 14:10 threatens and does not carry out.
9:1.text: And they spake unto all the company of the children of Israel, saying, The land, which we passed through to search it, is an exceeding good land.

provenance.other: 'Austere' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 19:21 and Luke 19:22, which are the servant's charge in the parable of the pounds and the nobleman's acceptance of it. The word occurs nowhere else in the Bible in English.
provenance.significance: Recover the parable and the borrowing pays. The austere man of Luke 19 is a nobleman who went into a far country to receive a kingdom, whose citizens sent a message after him saying 'We will not have this man to reign over us' — and whose last words in the parable are 'those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me' (19:27). Mosiah 9:2's austere man does exactly that: 'commanded that I should be slain'. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's only adjective for such a master and put it on a ruler who then performs the parable's closing act. The 1830 running text hyphenates the second adjective, 'blood-thirsty', and that word is a KJV rarity too — see the Proverbs 29:10 row on this verse.

9:2.note: 'But he being an austere and a blood-thirsty man, commanded that I should be slain.' Two words describe the ruler and both are KJV rarities: 'austere' belongs to Luke 19 alone and 'bloodthirsty' to Proverbs 29:10 alone. That a single clause should reach for both is the argument. Nothing else in the verse touches Luke, and the parable's subject — stewardship of money — has nothing to do with a war council in a wilderness; what has been taken is the character and the sentence he passes.
9:2.text: And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant. Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down, and reaping that I did not sow:

provenance.other: “bloodthirsty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 29:10. The KJV's usual idiom is periphrastic — 'bloody men' (Psalm 26:9, 59:2), 'the man of blood' — so the compound adjective is a single verse's property.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 29:10 reads in full: 'The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul.' Both halves of the proverb are in Mosiah 9:2. The bloodthirsty ruler hates the man who has just argued for sparing an enemy, and orders him killed; and someone — the verse does not say who — rescues him at the cost of much blood. A reader who recovers the proverb finds that the KJV's one bloodthirsty verse also contains the rescuer.

9:2.note: 'An austere and a blood-thirsty man.' The 1830 hyphenation preserves the word as a compound; the KJV prints it solid, once. Recorded at moderate rather than high because a single adjective is a slender thing to build on, and because 'bloodthirsty' was ordinary English in 1830 and needed no source — the reason for keeping the row is that the other adjective in the same phrase is also a KJV rarity, and that Proverbs 29:10's second clause describes what happens next in the verse.
9:2.text: The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul.

provenance.other: 'Against his brother' occurs in five KJV verses, of which only Isaiah 19:2 and Ezekiel 38:21 describe a civil war. Isaiah 19:2 is the only one built as a chain of identical nouns on either side of 'against' — 'every one against his brother, and every one against his neighbour; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom' — which is the construction Mosiah 9:2 uses. Within that verse, “every one against his brother” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and so does “city against city” — the construction is Isaiah 19:2's property even though the particular nouns Mosiah 9:2 puts either side of 'against' are not Isaiah's.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 19:2 is the oracle against Egypt, and what God does to Egypt in it is set it against itself. Mosiah 9:2 has a Nephite army destroying the greater part of itself in a wilderness over a question of policy toward the Lamanites — an internal war in a people who have just refused to be a nation of one mind. The chapter then spends itself on a colony founded by the survivors of that self-slaughter.

9:2.note: 'For father fought against father, and brother against brother, until the greatest number of our army was destroyed in the wilderness.' No phrase is reproduced; the borrowing, if it is one, is the KJV's formula for civil war — a noun repeated on both sides of 'against' — which Isaiah 19:2 establishes and Matthew 10:21 and Luke 12:53 vary with different nouns on each side ('the brother shall deliver up the brother', 'the father shall be divided against the son'). Isaiah's identical-noun form is what the Book of Mormon has.
9:2.whyNot: 'Brother against brother' is an English idiom for civil war independent of any verse, and the Book of Mormon's pairing is father/father and brother/brother where Isaiah's is brother/neighbour and city/city. The construction is shared; no words are.
9:2.text: And I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians: and they shall fight every one against his brother, and every one against his neighbour; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.

provenance.other: “let us go up at once” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 13:30, Caleb's answer to the evil report. “go up and possess” occurs in exactly two, Deuteronomy 1:21 and Deuteronomy 9:23, both of them Moses recalling the same episode. 'Possess it' on its own occurs in forty-six verses and identifies nothing.
provenance.significance: Caleb's 'Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it' is the sentence that gets Israel into the land a generation late, and Deuteronomy 9:23 is the sentence that judges the generation that would not act on it. Zeniff collects 'as many as were desirous to go up to possess the land' and is immediately smitten with famine 'for we were slow to remember the Lord our God' — which is Deuteronomy's verdict on the failed attempt at Numbers 14:40-45, where the people went up anyway, without the LORD among them, and were smitten. The type-scene begun at 9:1 completes here in its unfavourable half.

9:3.note: 'And yet, I being over zealous to inherit the land of our fathers, collected as many as were desirous to go up to possess the land … but we were smitten with famine and sore afflictions: for we were slow to remember the Lord our God.' The going-up-to-possess formula is Deuteronomic and Zeniff uses it with Caleb's confidence and Numbers 14:44's outcome. Confidence is moderate because the formula is common enough in Deuteronomy that no one verse can be isolated; what is not moderate is that the whole of 9:1-3 walks through Numbers 13-14 in order — spy, good report, dissent, near-death, and then a presumptuous ascent that is smitten.
9:3.text: And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.

provenance.other: “cunning craftiness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:14. The argument is made in full at Mosiah 7:21, where the phrase enters the book.
provenance.significance: The interest of the second occurrence is that it is in a different hand. Mosiah 7:21 is Limhi speaking to his people two generations later; Mosiah 9:10 is Zeniff's own record, which the book has just begun quoting verbatim. The two men use the same Pauline phrase for the same king's treaty, which within the fiction means Limhi got it from the record he has been reading and which for this catalogue means the borrowing is doing structural work rather than decorating a sentence.

9:10.note: 'Now, it was the cunning and the craftiness of king Laman, to bring my people into bondage, that he yielded up the land, that we might possess it.' The KJV's one 'cunning craftiness', used a second time of the same event by a different narrator. Under the standing rule a repeat within a book is registered rather than re-argued, and the argument is at 7:21; this row exists because Zeniff's account and Limhi's agree word for word about the deceit and because Ephesians 4:14's closing clause, 'whereby they lie in wait to deceive', is what this verse spells out.
9:10.text: That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;

provenance.route: Genesis 15:13 → Acts 7:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “bring them into bondage” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:6. Acts 7:6 is Stephen paraphrasing Genesis 15:13, and Genesis 15:13 does not contain the phrase: it reads 'they shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years'. The whole 'into bondage' family is four verses — Nehemiah 5:5, Acts 7:6, 2 Corinthians 11:20, Galatians 2:4 — and three of the four are New Testament.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's mediation finding, and the tool could not make it. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for Genesis 15:13 against Acts 7:6, because its alignment sets 'they should bring them into bondage' opposite Genesis's 'is not theirs' and so reports the Book of Mormon as reading neither. The rarity count decides what the alignment could not: the Old Testament's promise of Egyptian bondage says 'serve', and only the New Testament's retelling of it says 'bring them into bondage'. Mosiah 9:11 has Stephen's phrase, not Abraham's. And the substance follows: what Laman fears is that his immigrant population will 'wax strong in the land' and become unmanageable, which is Exodus 1:9-10's fear in Acts 7:17-19's words.

9:11.note: 'King Laman began to grow uneasy, lest by any means my people should wax strong in the land, and that they could not overpower them and bring them into bondage.' The KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, and it belongs to Stephen's speech — the same speech Mosiah 7:26 borrowed at its climax. Note also what the mediation does to the chapter's politics: Zeniff's colony is cast in the position of Israel in Egypt, growing too numerous for a king who then enslaves it, and the language used for the enslavement is the language of the Bible's own great retelling of that story rather than of the story itself.
9:11.text: And God spake on this wise, That his seed should sojourn in a strange land; and that they should bring them into bondage, and entreat them evil four hundred years.

provenance.other: “deal wisely” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 1:10, where it is Pharaoh's euphemism for what he is about to do. 'Subtilly' occurs in three (1 Samuel 23:22, Psalm 105:25, Acts 7:19), of which Acts 7:19 and Psalm 105:25 both describe the same Egyptian policy — so the KJV has three separate words for it and the Book of Mormon uses none of them, choosing Ephesians 4:14's 'cunning craftiness' instead.
provenance.significance: Exodus 1:8-14 is the template for Mosiah 9:9-12 point by point and in order: the immigrants multiply and prosper (9:9, Exodus 1:7); a king fears they will grow too strong (9:11, Exodus 1:9-10); he deals craftily rather than openly (9:10, Exodus 1:10); and the object is forced labour, so that the host nation may live off the work of their hands (9:12, Exodus 1:11-14). The one element the Book of Mormon adds is the treaty — Laman gives the land away in order to get the people into it — which makes the deceit contractual rather than merely administrative, and which is why the borrowed word for it comes from Ephesians rather than from Exodus.

9:11.note: 'Lest by any means my people should wax strong in the land, and that they could not overpower them and bring them into bondage.' Pharaoh's calculation, in the Book of Mormon's words: Exodus 1:10 reads 'let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply … and so get them up out of the land.' The 'lest' clause with a demographic fear inside it is the shared structure, and the sequence around it is Exodus 1's. No phrase of Exodus is reproduced, which is why the row is conceptual; the reproduced phrase in this verse is Acts 7:6's and is catalogued separately.
9:11.text: Come on, let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply, and it come to pass, that, when there falleth out any war, they join also unto our enemies, and fight against us, and so get them up out of the land.

provenance.other: “bring us into bondage” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 2:4 — the first person plural, as against Acts 7:6's 'bring them into bondage' at Mosiah 9:11. The Book of Mormon uses each pronoun in its correct grammatical setting: Laman's intention toward a third party at 9:11, and the colony's own account of what was intended toward them at 9:12.
provenance.significance: Galatians 2:4 is the sentence that names Paul's opponents 'false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage'. Set it beside Mosiah 9 and the whole chapter is in it. Zeniff opens the chapter as a man sent to spy (9:1); Laman brings his people in under a treaty rather than openly (9:6-7, 9:10); and the object throughout is to bring them into bondage. One Pauline verse holds the spying, the false dealing and the enslavement that the chapter takes nineteen verses to narrate — and the reader who recovers it finds that in Galatians the bondage is a religious one and the liberty is Christ's.

9:12.note: 'They were desirous to bring us into bondage, that they might glut themselves with the labors of our hands.' A KJV singleton, and the pronoun is right: 'us' here where 9:11 had Acts 7:6's 'them', which is the discrimination ADJUDICATING §4 warns is the adjudicator's to catch and not the tool's. 'Glut' is not a KJV word in any form — the KJV has 'glutton' and 'gluttonous' — so the vivid half of the sentence is the Book of Mormon's own.
9:12.text: And that because of false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage:

provenance.other: “feed themselves” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezekiel 34:2 and Ezekiel 34:10, both in the shepherd oracle and both meaning that those who should feed a flock are eating it instead.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 34 is already the source at Mosiah 8:21, five verses earlier in the same reading, where Limhi's people are a wild flock devoured by beasts. Mosiah 9:12 turns the same chapter's other half on the Lamanites: they mean to 'feast themselves upon the flocks of our fields', which is Ezekiel's charge against shepherds who feed themselves and not the flocks. Two consecutive chapters of Mosiah reach into the same oracle for opposite ends of the figure — the flock at 8:21 and the eaters at 9:12.

9:12.note: 'Yea, that they might feast themselves upon the flocks of our fields.' 'Feast' is not Ezekiel's verb and the flocks here are literal livestock rather than a people, so the contact is a reflexive construction and a noun; that is an echo and no more. It is recorded because Ezekiel 34 is demonstrably in view in this stretch of the book — Mosiah 8:21 takes its shepherdless scattered flock from Ezekiel 34:5 — and because the Lamanites' offence in this verse is exactly the one Ezekiel 34 exists to condemn.
9:12.whyNot: Two words, one of them a common reflexive, and the sense is different: Ezekiel's shepherds eat the flock they were given to keep, while the Lamanites eat a flock that was never theirs. Without the Ezekiel 34:5 borrowing one chapter earlier there would be nothing here to record.
9:12.text: Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?

provenance.other: “in the strength of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 71:16 and Micah 5:4. Micah's is 'he shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD'; Psalm 71:16's is 'I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD'. The Book of Mormon's verb is 'go' — 'in the strength of the Lord did we go forth to battle' — which is the Psalm's and not Micah's.
provenance.significance: Psalm 71 is an old man's prayer not to be forsaken when his strength fails, and 71:16 is his resolution to go in a strength that is not his own and to make mention of God's righteousness 'even of thine only'. Zeniff's army is outnumbered and armed with whatever it could invent (9:16); the psalm it is quoting is about having nothing left to go in. The next verse says God heard, which is what Psalm 71 is asking for.

9:17.note: 'Yea, in the strength of the Lord did we go forth to battle against the Lamanites.' Of the KJV's two occurrences of the phrase, one has the Book of Mormon's verb and one does not, and the discrimination is worth making because the phrase becomes a formula in the corpus after this. The rest of the verse is the chapter's own: 'cry mightily to the Lord' is Jonah 3:8's and is catalogued separately, and 'deliver us out of the hands of our enemies' is close to Luke 1:74's 'delivered out of the hand of our enemies' but has the plural where Luke has the singular and Judges 8:34 has the plural, so no source is isolable there.
9:17.text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

provenance.other: “cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8, the king of Nineveh's decree. The KJV's other intensifiers for prayer are 'cried with a loud voice' and 'cried unto the LORD', neither of which is this adverb.
provenance.significance: Jonah 3:8 is a king's proclamation to a doomed city: let man and beast be covered with sackcloth and cry mightily unto God, and let them turn from their evil way — and in the next verse the question is whether God will turn and repent so that they perish not. Mosiah 9:17-18 is a king's account of his own people crying mightily and being heard. The suppressed correspondence is that Jonah 3's criers are the enemy nation, spared against the prophet's wishes; Zeniff opens this chapter by arguing that the enemy nation should be spared.

9:17.note: 'For I and my people did cry mightily to the Lord, that he would deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.' The KJV's one 'cry mightily', in a verse that is itself a king's edict about how a people in danger should pray. Zeniff is a king reporting that his people did it. The phrase is short and the setting is different — sackcloth and repentance in Jonah, a battle line here — but the adverb has one home in the KJV and the Book of Mormon has borrowed it into another king's mouth.
9:17.text: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.

provenance.other: “forth in his might” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 5:31 — 'let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might'. The antecedent of 'his' there is the sun, not God, which is the reason for the moderate confidence.
provenance.significance: Judges 5:31 is the last line of the Song of Deborah, a victory song after an outnumbered Israelite force destroyed a superior army: 'So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD.' Mosiah 9:18 is the same sentence in prose — God heard, we went forth in his might, we slew them until we had driven them out of our land — and the chapter ends, as Judges 5:31 does, with a count and a rest. The suppressed correspondence is that Judges 5's victory is won by a woman with a tent peg and celebrated in a poem; Zeniff's is won with cimeters and clubs and counted to the man.

9:18.note: 'And God did hear our cries, and did answer our prayers; and we did go forth in his might.' Four words from the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, at the end of the Bible's other outnumbered-army battle report. The Book of Mormon shifts the possessive from the sun to God, which is a real change of sense and keeps this at moderate; what recommends the row is that the phrase has exactly one home and that Judges 5:31 is the closing formula of exactly this kind of narrative.
9:18.text: So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might. And the land had rest forty years.

provenance.other: “great lamentation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:2 — 'And devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him.' Genesis 50:10's mourning for Jacob is 'a great and very sore lamentation', and Zechariah 12:11 has 'a great mourning'; neither is this phrase.
provenance.significance: Acts 8:2 is the burial of Stephen, and it stands eight verses after Acts 7:52 — the verse Limhi borrows at Mosiah 7:26 to say that his fathers slew the prophet who foretold the coming of Christ. Within this three-chapter stretch the Book of Mormon has taken the climax of Stephen's speech and the sentence about his burial, in that order: the prophet killed for announcing the Just One at 7:26, and the men burying their dead with great lamentation at 9:19. The pairing is not visible from either verse alone. Note too what Acts 8:2 supplies that this verse needs: it is the KJV's one place where the burying and the lamenting are done by the same hands, which is Zeniff's whole point — 'I, myself, with mine own hands, did help to bury their dead.'

9:19.note: 'And I, myself, with mine own hands, did help to bury their dead. And behold, to our great sorrow and lamentation, two hundred and seventy-nine of our brethren were slain.' The KJV's one 'great lamentation' is a burial verse, and this is a burial verse. 'With mine own hands' is in no KJV verse — the nearest is Philemon 1:19's 'with mine own hand', of writing — so the borrowing is the lamentation and not the hands. The chapter closes on a count of the dead, and the source it closes on is the burial of the man whose speech opened Limhi's sermon two chapters earlier.
9:19.text: And devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him.
